claims.text: An adaptive, multi-fidelity free-energy integration scheme with on-the-fly machine-learning corrections can substantially reduce the cost of calculating fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
The proposed scheme can retain the full vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration contributions to phase free energies.
Accurate free energies are required for both solid and liquid phases near melting.
The protocol will use fast data-driven sampling with periodic high-fidelity ab initio anchor calculations.
Ab initio anchor calculations will capture regions with high anharmonicity and strong electron–vibration coupling.
The method will be tested from approximately 0.8 to 1.2 times the melting temperature.
Calibration will begin with elemental and binary systems before extension to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Adaptive integration will concentrate computational effort on the most challenging regions of the free-energy landscape.
Machine learning will interpolate over less critical regions of the free-energy landscape.
The machine-learning model will rapidly sample the free-energy landscape and identify likely low-error regions.
Selective ab initio calculations in regions with large anharmonic or electron–vibration effects will ensure that critical free-energy contributions are captured accurately.
Coupling machine-learning sampling to selective ab initio calculations will reduce overall simulation time.
Fusion free energies, latent heats, and fusion entropies will have accuracy comparable to full explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed method may provide a speed-up of several orders of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed method will be significantly faster than TOR-TILD, especially for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
TOR-TILD is efficient only for simpler systems.
The method is expected to be reliable for systems with moderate to high anharmonicity and electron–vibration coupling within 0.8–1.2 T_m.
Performance for systems with extreme or unexpected behavior remains unvalidated.
The speed-up and error tolerance will depend on system complexity and machine-learning training-data quality.
Machine-learning interatomic potentials can approach underlying DFT accuracy for elemental and multicomponent systems while providing a favorable balance between accuracy and computational cost.
